For Sainz, a two-time world rally champion who entered the day leading the field after six previous stage victories, his bid to capture his first-ever Dakar title came to an abrupt end. Just 79 kilometers into the stage, his Volkswagen slammed into a dried-up riverbed. His French navigator, Michel Perin, sustained a shoulder injury, and the pair required helicopter evacuation for medical treatment.

Speaking to PA Sport, Perin explained the circumstances: "We had made a small mistake in the first part. We took the wrong direction at a Y crossing but it was not too bad because we did end up on the right trail. We were tailing Giniel De Villiers, who had started about 10 minutes after us, so it was still sort of okay. There was a hidden way-point indicated as 'danger'—but it should have been indicated as 'extremely dangerous.'" He continued, "The car behind us, Nani Roma's car, would have fallen in the same hole as we did if we had not been there already. I'm okay, I just have something broken in my arm, but I'm all right."

De Villiers described the challenging conditions: "It was really a tough stage. In places we would go around in circles for 15 minutes to find the right trail. It was very dangerous and the sand was really soft. We stopped one time to deflate our tyres, then a second time in a huge canyon with tons of boulders. My co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz had to get out of the car to find a way out. It was really a tough day."

Miller echoed these sentiments, calling it an especially punishing stage: "I can tell you that this was a very demanding stage. I cannot even imagine how the amateurs will make it to the finish today. It was not just difficult, navigation was almost impossible. It was a long series of horror situations from start to finish. These were the longest 200km in my life. The sun and the sand were so bright that I could not see anything." Regarding his rival's misfortune, Miller added, "It's not good news to know that Carlos had to withdraw. He has an important place in the team."

Over in the motorcycle division, defending champion Cyril Despres of KTM kept alive his pursuit of a third consecutive title by winning his third stage of the rally, clocking in at 3:57:37 and moving up to second place overall. Despres's teammate from Spain, Marc Coma, wasn't about to make things simple for the Frenchman, though—Coma finished the stage just 1:23 behind him, preserving his overall lead with a substantial cushion of 1:29:48.

This twelfth stage proved to be the toughest test yet since the rally launched on January 3rd in Buenos Aires, as competitors battled through sand dunes and rainfall in the western regions of Argentina. Prior to this stage, Sainz had enjoyed a strong hold on first place overall, having triumphed in six of the ten preceding stages.

# Dakar Rally Chaos: Dramatic Stage 12 Sees Multiple Crashes as Field Battles Brutal Terrain

**[Dateline] —** The penultimate stage of this year's Dakar Rally delivered high drama today as treacherous dune sections and unpredictable terrain sent shockwaves through the standings, with several top contenders suffering crashes that reshaped the fight for overall victory.

Stage 12, a grueling 412-kilometer special stretching across some of the rally's most unforgiving desert landscape, saw at least three major incidents in the car and truck categories, forcing organizers to deploy medical helicopters to two separate locations.

## Chaos in the Dunes

The first major incident occurred just 87 kilometers into the special when a leading prototype vehicle rolled multiple times after cresting a blind dune at high speed. The driver, visibly shaken but uninjured, described the terrifying moment.

"I saw the crest and thought I knew what was on the other side—I didn't," said the driver, still catching his breath as recovery crews worked on his vehicle. "The car just left the ground and everything went sideways. You lose all sense of direction when you're rolling like that. I just braced and hoped for the best."

His co-driver, who suffered a minor shoulder injury in the incident, remained remarkably composed when speaking to reporters.

"We train for this, but nothing really prepares you for the reality of it," the co-driver said. "The notes said 'caution, dune, blind crest'—but at that speed, on that terrain, caution only gets you so far. I'm just grateful we're both walking away from this."

## A Costly Setback for the Overall Standings

Perhaps the most consequential crash of the day involved one of the pre-race favorites, whose hopes for the overall title suffered a severe blow when his vehicle became stuck in a soft sand trap before rolling while attempting to extract itself.

"This is Dakar—this is what happens," the driver reflected afterward, visibly frustrated but philosophical. "One moment you're fighting for the stage win, the next you're fighting just to get the car pointed the right way again. We lost probably 45 minutes, maybe more. The overall standings, I think, are gone for us now. But we finished. That's what matters today."

His co-driver, who has partnered with him for the past four Dakar campaigns, offered a more emotional take on the ordeal.

"It's heartbreaking, honestly," he admitted. "We worked so hard all rally to be in position, and then the desert reminds you who's really in charge out here. But we dug the car out ourselves, no outside assistance, and we crossed that finish line. There's pride in that, even on a day like today."

## Truck Category Drama

The truck category wasn't spared either, as a veteran team experienced a dramatic rollover on a fast, rutted section in the stage's closing kilometers. Remarkably, both crew members walked away without serious injury, and after inspection, they were able to continue.

"These trucks are built like tanks, and today I was very thankful for that," the driver said with a tired smile. "We hit a rut we didn't see, and the truck just went over. My co-driver and I looked at each other, made sure we were both okay, and then we got out and started figuring out how to get her back on her wheels."

## Looking Ahead

Despite the day's carnage, rally director confirmed that all affected competitors were cleared by medical staff and that the final stage would proceed as scheduled. With the overall leaderboard now dramatically reshuffled, tomorrow's final stage promises to be a fitting, tension-filled conclusion to what has already been one of the most unpredictable editions of the Dakar Rally in recent memory.

"Dakar doesn't care about your plans," one veteran competitor summed up. "It only cares about respect. Today, a lot of us learned that lesson the hard way."

---

*Final stage standings and results to follow as competitors prepare for tomorrow's concluding special.*
